content: IgA nephropathy is the most common form of glomerulonephritis globally. It leads to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in approximately 15% to 20% of patients within 10 years of diagnosis and in 30% to 40% of patients within 20 years. This review aimed to evaluate the benefits and risks of immunosuppressive treatments for IgA nephropathy. The review included 58 studies with a total of 3,933 randomized participants, including six studies involving children. The studies varied significantly in terms of disease characteristics, such as kidney function and proteinuria levels. Most studies on steroid therapy included patients with proteinuria levels of 1 g/day or higher. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was high or unclear across many methodological domains. In patients with IgA nephropathy and proteinuria greater than 1 g/day, corticosteroid therapy administered over two to four months with a tapering course likely reduces the risk of progression to ESKD compared to placebo or standard care (moderate-certainty evidence). Steroid therapy may also increase the likelihood of complete remission, reduce the risk of doubling serum creatinine (SCr), and lower urinary protein excretion, although the certainty of evidence for these outcomes is low. However, the effects of steroid therapy on glomerular filtration rate (GFR), mortality, infection, and malignancy remain uncertain. The risk of adverse events associated with steroid therapy is unclear due to variability in the types of steroid regimens used and the rarity of reported events. Cytotoxic agents, such as azathioprine (AZA) or cyclophosphamide (CPA), either alone or in combination with steroids, showed uncertain effects on ESKD progression, complete remission, GFR, and proteinuria. Doubling of SCr was not reported in these studies. The evidence for these outcomes was of low or very low certainty. Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) demonstrated uncertain effects on ESKD progression, complete remission, doubling of SCr, GFR, proteinuria, infection, and malignancy. Mortality was not reported in studies evaluating MMF. Calcineurin inhibitors, when compared to placebo or standard care, showed uncertain effects on complete remission, SCr, GFR, proteinuria, infection, and malignancy. ESKD and mortality outcomes were not reported. Mizoribine, used alongside renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, had uncertain effects on ESKD progression, complete remission, GFR, proteinuria, infection, and malignancy. Mortality and SCr outcomes were not reported. Leflunomide, followed by a tapering course of oral prednisone, compared to prednisone alone, showed uncertain effects on ESKD progression, complete remission, doubling of SCr, GFR, proteinuria, and infection. Mortality and malignancy outcomes were not reported. The effects of other immunosuppressive regimens, including combinations of steroids with non-immunosuppressive agents or mTOR inhibitors, were inconclusive due to insufficient data and low or very low certainty evidence. The impact of treatments on mortality, malignancy, significant GFR reduction, and adverse events was highly uncertain. Subgroup analyses to assess the influence of specific patient characteristics, such as ethnicity or disease severity, on treatment effectiveness were not feasible due to a lack of sufficient studies. In conclusion, corticosteroid therapy likely prevents GFR decline or doubling of SCr in patients with IgA nephropathy and proteinuria. However, evidence regarding the effects of other immunosuppressive agents, such as CPA, AZA, or MMF, on clinical outcomes is sparse and of low quality. The adverse effects of steroid therapy remain uncertain due to limited and inconsistent data. Further research is needed to identify patient subgroups that may benefit most from specific treatments and to better understand the risks and benefits of immunosuppressive therapies in IgA nephropathy.
